Under Law 15, a goal cannot be scored directly from a throw-in; if the ball enters the opponents' goal directly from a throw-in, a goal kick is awarded. Blue restarts with a goal kick and no sanction applies.

Under Law 12, a reckless trip is a direct free kick offence that must be cautioned (yellow card), and because it occurred inside the offender's own penalty area, a penalty kick is awarded to Red (Law 14). Since there was no goal-scoring opportunity, the DOGSO provisions do not apply, so the sanction remains a caution for recklessness.

Under Law 12, a reckless trip is a direct free kick offence and a caution for unsporting behaviour; because it occurred inside the defender's own penalty area, a penalty kick is awarded to Red (Law 14). With no obvious goal-scoring opportunity, there is no DOGSO consideration, so the yellow card for recklessness stands.

Under Law 12, tripping an opponent recklessly is a direct free kick offence, and because it occurred inside the defender's own penalty area, a penalty kick is awarded (Law 14). A reckless challenge requires a caution (yellow card); there is no DOGSO consideration because the attacker was moving away from goal with no goal-scoring opportunity.
Under Law 8, a goal may be scored directly against the opponents from the kick-off, so the goal is awarded to Red. Play restarts with a kick-off taken by Blue.
Under Law 8, a goal may be scored directly against the opponents from a kick-off, so Red's goal stands. Play restarts with a kick-off taken by Blue.
Under Law 8, a goal may be scored directly against the opponents from a kick-off, so the goal stands for Red. Play restarts with a kick-off taken by Blue.

Under Law 17, a corner kick is awarded when the whole ball passes over the goal line, without a goal being scored, having last touched a player of the defending team. The Blue defender's deflection was the last touch, so Red restarts with a corner kick and no offence occurred.

Under Law 17, a corner kick is awarded when the whole of the ball passes over the goal line, without a goal being scored, having last been touched by a player of the defending team. The Blue defender's deflection was the last touch, so Red restarts with a corner kick.

Under Law 17, a corner kick is awarded when the whole ball passes over the goal line, without a goal being scored, having last touched a player of the defending team. The deflection off the Blue defender means Red restarts with a corner kick; no offence occurred, so there is no sanction.

Deliberately punching an opponent in the face is violent conduct under Law 12, so the Blue player is sent off. Because the ball was in play and the offence was against an opponent on the field, Red is awarded a direct free kick from the position of the offence in midfield (Law 13), even though it happened away from the ball.

Deliberately punching an opponent while the ball is in play is violent conduct, a sending-off offence under Law 12. Because the offence is committed against an opponent on the field, Red are awarded a direct free kick from where the punch occurred, regardless of where the ball was (Laws 12 and 13).

Deliberately punching an opponent while the ball is in play is violent conduct under Law 12, so the Blue player is sent off with a red card. Because the offence was against an opponent on the field, Red is awarded a direct free kick from where the punch happened in midfield (Law 13). It does not matter that the ball was elsewhere.
Under Law 11, there is no offside offence if a player receives the ball directly from a throw-in, so play continues. Law 15 likewise lists no offside offence among throw-in restrictions.
Under Law 11, there is no offside offence if a player receives the ball directly from a throw-in, so play continues. Law 15 also confirms that no offside applies directly from a throw-in.
Under Law 11, there is no offside offence if a player receives the ball directly from a throw-in, so play continues. Law 15 has the same exemption.

Under Law 12, a goalkeeper who handles the ball inside their own penalty area after it has been deliberately kicked to them by a teammate commits an offence punished by an indirect free kick. The kick is taken from where the offence occurred, subject to Law 13's rule that an indirect free kick inside the goal area is taken from the goal area line nearest the offence. No disciplinary sanction applies because no goal-scoring opportunity was denied.

Under Law 12, a goalkeeper commits an indirect free kick offence by touching the ball with the hands inside their own penalty area after it has been deliberately kicked to them by a team-mate. Red is awarded an indirect free kick from where the handling occurred, subject to Law 13: if that point is inside the goal area, the kick is taken from the goal area line parallel to the goal line, at the point nearest to where the offence occurred. No sanction applies because no goal-scoring opportunity was denied.

Under Law 12, a goalkeeper who handles the ball inside their own penalty area after a teammate deliberately kicks it to them commits an offence. Red is awarded an indirect free kick from where the goalkeeper handled the ball. No disciplinary sanction applies because no goal-scoring opportunity was denied.

Under Law 11, a player in an offside position who receives the ball from an opponent who deliberately played it, other than a deliberate save, is not considered to have gained an advantage. A poorly executed (miskicked) deliberate pass is still a deliberate play, so the Red forward commits no offside offence and play continues.

Under Law 11, a player in an offside position who receives the ball from an opponent who deliberately played it is not considered to have gained an advantage, unless it was a deliberate save. The Blue defender, under no pressure, deliberately played the ball, and a misjudged pass or miskick still counts as a deliberate play. The Red forward is therefore not penalised for offside and play continues.

Under Law 11, a player in an offside position who receives the ball from an opponent who deliberately played it (other than a deliberate save) has not gained an advantage. The defender's controlled but poorly executed pass is still a deliberate play, so the Red forward is not penalised and play continues.

Under Law 13, once the ball is kicked and clearly moves it is in play, and the kicker may not touch it again before another player has touched it. A second touch is an offence, penalised by an indirect free kick to Blue from where the second touch occurred (Law 13; Law 13.2). No sanction applies unless the second touch was itself a handball or stopped a promising attack.

Under Law 13, once the ball is in play from a free kick (kicked and clearly moving), the kicker must not touch it again until another player has touched it. A second touch is an offence, so Blue is awarded an indirect free kick from where the second touch occurred. No disciplinary sanction applies unless the second touch was itself a handball or another offence.

Under Law 13 (and Law 9/12 principles), once a free kick is taken the ball is in play when kicked and clearly moves, and the kicker must not touch it again before it has touched another player. A second touch by the kicker is penalised with an indirect free kick to Blue from where the second touch occurred; no sanction applies unless the second touch was itself a handball or other disciplinary offence.

Under Law 14, the penalty kicker must not play the ball again until it has touched another player; rebounding off the goalpost does not count. Blue is awarded an indirect free kick from where the kicker touched the ball a second time, with no disciplinary sanction.

Under Law 14, once the penalty kick is taken the kicker must not play the ball again until it has touched another player; the post does not count. Blue is awarded an indirect free kick from where the second touch occurred, and no disciplinary sanction is required.

Under Law 14, once the penalty kick is taken the kicker must not play the ball again until it has touched another player. A rebound off the goalpost does not count as a touch by another player, so the kicker's second touch is an offence. Blue are awarded an indirect free kick where the second touch occurred, and no disciplinary sanction is required.

Under Law 3, a substitute who enters the field without the referee's permission and interferes with play is penalised with a direct free kick to the opponents (Blue) from the position of the interference. Under Law 12, entering the field of play without permission is a cautionable offence, so the substitute is shown a yellow card.

Under Law 3, if a substitute enters the field of play without the referee's permission and interferes with play, play is stopped and restarted with a direct free kick at the position of the interference. Under Law 12, the substitute is cautioned for entering without permission. Blue therefore takes the free kick where the pass was stopped.

Under Law 3, if a substitute enters the field of play without the referee's permission and interferes with play, play is restarted with a direct free kick at the position of the interference. Under Law 12, the substitute is cautioned for entering the field of play without the referee's permission.

Under Law 8, when play is stopped for an injury with no offence and the ball is inside the penalty area, the restart is a dropped ball to the defending team's goalkeeper in their own penalty area, regardless of who last touched it. Play restarts with a dropped ball to Blue's goalkeeper; all other players must be at least 4 m away until the ball is in play.

Under Law 8, when play is stopped with no offence and the ball is inside the penalty area, it is dropped for the defending team's goalkeeper in their penalty area, regardless of who last touched it. All other players must be at least 4 m away until the ball is in play.

Under Law 8, when play is stopped with the ball inside the penalty area and no offence has occurred, the restart is a dropped ball for the defending team's goalkeeper in their penalty area. Who last touched the ball does not matter. Play therefore restarts with a dropped ball to Blue's goalkeeper, and all other players must be at least 4m away.

Under Law 12.2, a goalkeeper who controls the ball with the hands for more than eight seconds (after the referee's visible five-second countdown) concedes a corner kick to the opposing team. No disciplinary sanction applies.

Under Law 12, a goalkeeper who controls the ball with the hands for more than eight seconds inside their own penalty area concedes a corner kick to the opposing team. The referee signals this with a visual five-second countdown. No disciplinary sanction applies, so Red restarts with a corner kick.

Under Law 12.2, a goalkeeper who controls the ball with the hands for more than eight seconds is penalised with a corner kick to the opposing team. The referee should use a visible five-second countdown before awarding it, and no disciplinary sanction applies.

Under Law 13 (and Law 10), a goal cannot be scored directly against the kicking team from a free kick. If the ball goes directly into the kicker's own goal, a corner kick is awarded to the opponents, so Blue gets a corner kick.
Under Law 13, a goal cannot be scored directly from a free kick into the kicker's own goal. If the ball enters the kicker's own goal directly, a corner kick is awarded to the opposing team, Blue.
Under Law 13, a goal cannot be scored directly from a free kick into the kicker's own goal. If the ball enters the kicking team's own goal directly, a corner kick is awarded to the opponents (Blue).

Under Law 12, when a defender denies an obvious goal-scoring opportunity by committing a foul inside their own penalty area while making a genuine attempt to play the ball, a penalty kick is awarded and the sanction is reduced from a sending-off to a caution (yellow card). Red restarts with a penalty kick.

Under Law 12, when a defender commits a DOGSO offence inside their own penalty area while making a genuine attempt to play the ball, a penalty kick is awarded and the sanction is downgraded from a sending-off to a caution. Red receives the penalty kick and the Blue defender is shown a yellow card.

Under Law 12, when a defender commits a DOGSO offence inside their own penalty area that is an attempt to play the ball, a penalty kick is awarded and the sanction is reduced from a red card to a caution (yellow card). Red is awarded the penalty kick.

Under Law 12, it is a handball offence for a player to score in the opponents' goal directly from their hand or arm, even if the contact is accidental. The goal is disallowed and Blue is awarded a direct free kick where the ball hit the arm. There is no disciplinary sanction because the handball was accidental.

Under Law 12, a player commits a handball offence if they score in the opponents' goal directly from their hand/arm, even if the contact is accidental. The goal is disallowed and Blue restarts with a direct free kick from where the contact occurred. No caution is given because the handball was accidental.

Under Law 12, it is a handball offence for a player to score in the opponents' goal directly from their hand or arm, even if the contact is accidental, so the goal is disallowed. Blue restarts with a direct free kick from where the ball touched the arm. No caution is given because the handball was accidental.

Under the 2026/27 Law 15 amendment, when a thrower delays the throw-in, the referee may start a visual five-second countdown. If the throw-in is not taken before the countdown ends, the throw-in is awarded to the opposing team. Blue therefore takes the throw-in, and the loss of possession replaces a caution for delay.

Under the 2026/27 Law 15 amendment, if the referee judges a throw-in is being delayed and starts the visual five-second countdown, failure to take it before the countdown ends means the throw-in is awarded to the opposing team. Blue therefore restarts with a throw-in from the same place. The countdown procedure is the remedy here, so no caution is required.

Under the 2026/27 Law 15 amendment, when the referee judges a throw-in is being deliberately delayed, they start a visual five-second countdown. If the throw-in is not taken before it expires, the throw-in is awarded to the opposing team, so Blue takes it from the same place.

Under the 2026/27 Law 16 time-wasting provision, once the referee starts the visual five-second countdown for a delayed goal kick and the kick is not taken in time, the opposing team is awarded a corner kick. Red therefore restarts with a corner kick, and no caution is required for this offence itself.

Under the 2026/27 Law 16 amendment, if the referee judges a goal kick is being delayed, they begin a visual five-second countdown. If the kick has not been taken when the countdown ends, a corner kick is awarded to the opposing team (Red). The restart change is itself the penalty for the time-wasting, so no caution is required.

Under the 2026/27 Law 16 amendment, once the referee has started a visual five-second countdown for a delayed goal kick and it is not taken in time, a corner kick is awarded to the opposing team. Red therefore restarts with a corner kick, and the expiry of the countdown carries no automatic caution.

Under Law 14, if the kicker accidentally plays the ball twice, for example by slipping so that it touches the non-kicking foot immediately after the kick, and the ball enters the goal, the penalty kick is retaken. The double touch is accidental, so no disciplinary sanction applies.

Under Law 14, if the penalty taker slips and accidentally touches the ball a second time with the non-kicking foot (a double touch) and the ball goes into the goal, the goal is disallowed and the kick is retaken. Because the touch was accidental, no disciplinary sanction is given.

Under Law 14, if the kicker slips and accidentally touches the ball with the non-kicking foot (an unintentional double touch) immediately after the kick and the ball enters the goal, the goal is disallowed and the penalty kick is retaken. No sanction is given because the touch was accidental.

Under Law 14, if the kicker slips and the ball accidentally touches their other foot immediately after the kick, the kick is retaken only if it is scored. Because this kick was saved, play is stopped and an indirect free kick is awarded to Blue. No caution is issued because the double touch was accidental.

Under Law 14, when the kicker accidentally touches the ball twice (e.g., slips and it hits the other foot) at a penalty kick, the kick is retaken only if a goal is scored. Since this kick was saved, play is stopped and restarted with an indirect free kick to Blue. No sanction applies because the double touch was accidental.

Under Law 14 (as amended from 2025/26), when the kicker accidentally touches the ball a second time, for example by slipping so the ball strikes their non-kicking foot, the kick is retaken only if it is scored. Because this kick was saved, it is not retaken. Play is stopped and Blue restarts with an indirect free kick, with no sanction since the touch was accidental.

The advantage was correctly applied and Red scored, so the goal stands and Blue restarts with a kick-off (Law 10). Under Law 12, when advantage is played for a DOGSO offence and a goal results, the offender is not sent off but is cautioned for unsporting behaviour.

The referee correctly applied advantage and Red scored, so the goal stands and play restarts with a kick-off (Law 10). Under Law 12, when advantage is played for a DOGSO offence, the sending-off is reduced to a caution for unsporting behaviour, so the Blue defender is cautioned.

The referee correctly applied advantage (Law 5/12), and the goal stands, so Blue restarts with a kick-off. Under Law 12, when advantage is played for a DOGSO offence and a goal results, the offender is not sent off but is cautioned for unsporting behaviour, with the yellow card shown when the ball is next out of play.
